title: The Model Isn’t Wrong—You’re Just Bad at Prompting
talk_summary: A prompt-engineering vendor talk covering Chain-of-Thought, few-shot prompting, meta-prompting, and how reasoning models differ from standard models. The most concrete, mechanism-backed claims are that few-shot examples give most of their benefit with 1-2 diverse examples (and can degrade past that), and that reasoning models should get minimal prompting without few-shot examples or explicit reasoning instructions.

takeaways.what_they_do: For reasoning models, skip few-shot examples and explicit 'think step by step' instructions; give a clear task description and let built-in reasoning do the work, encouraging more reasoning only if performance lags.
takeaways.evidence_quote: avoid fre shot prompting if you're going to do it start with like one one maybe only two examples

takeaways.what_they_do: When examples are needed (style/tone/format mimicry), use only one or two diverse examples covering expected input variety; more examples show diminishing and sometimes negative returns.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you get most of the gains from just like an example or two
takeaways.numbers: performance can degrade past a small number of examples (no specific figure given)

takeaways.what_they_do: Use an LLM to draft/refine prompts, but run a different meta-prompt per model provider because a prompt good for one provider may not suit another.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a prompt that is good for opening ey models might not be the same as anthropic and so we we tailor it a little bit for you

takeaways.technique: Spend bounded time on prompt before adding complexity
takeaways.what_they_do: Try the simplest prompt fix first (roughly an hour of iteration) before building RAG or complex pipelines, since simple prompts are easier to maintain.
takeaways.evidence_quote: just spending an hour trying to mess around with the prompt and then determining that you know it's impossible
